content: 1. Acyclovir 500 mg was administered twice daily for a duration of 3 days, as reported in the study by Patel in 1997. 2. Valaciclovir 500 mg was given once daily for 16 weeks, as described in the same study. 3. Valaciclovir 500 mg was prescribed twice daily for 5 days, as noted in the study by Reitano in 1998. 4. Valaciclovir was administered in varying doses (250 mg, 500 mg, or 1 g) either once daily or 250 mg twice daily for a year, as per the study by Reitano in 1998. 5. Valaciclovir was used episodically for 5 days, as reported in the study by Sekhin in 2004. 6. Valaciclovir 500 mg was given once daily for 8 months, as described in the same study. 7. Valaciclovir 500 mg was prescribed twice daily for 5 days, as noted in the study. 8. Suppressive antiviral therapy was compared to episodic antiviral therapy in four randomized trials. The risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, and imprecision were not serious. In two studies involving 229 patients, the mean and median times to the first recurrent episode were greater than 60 days or 185 days with suppressive therapy, compared to 32–46 days with episodic therapy. 9. In 383 patients, suppressive therapy resulted in 200 fewer recurrences per 1,000 people at 40 days compared to episodic therapy. The quality of evidence was moderate, and the recommendation was critical. 10. WHO guidelines (Recommendations 5 and 6) for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus emphasize the importance of suppressive therapy. 11. Quality of life improved from baseline in both treatment arms (80 patients total), with slightly greater improvement in the suppressive therapy group. However, these differences were not statistically significant. The quality of evidence was low, and the recommendation was critical. 12. Compliance with suppressive therapy was high. In one study, 70% of participants reported taking at least 95% of prescribed doses. In another study with 152 patients, 82–93% were at least 80% compliant. In a third study with 384 patients, 80% took over 80% of the medication. 13. One study compared suppressive therapy to true episodic therapy in 80 patients, with similar average medication intake (~90%). 14. Serious side effects unrelated to the drug were reported in 2,364 patients receiving suppressive therapy and 1,097 receiving episodic therapy. One serious side effect occurred with suppressive therapy but was not drug-related. 15. In randomized trials, no serious adverse events were reported with suppressive valaciclovir therapy. In one study, grade 2 neutropenia was observed in a single arm. 16. Famciclovir 250 mg twice daily for 6 months was compared to 125 mg twice daily for 5 days in suppressive versus episodic therapy, as reported in the Bartlett 2008 study. 17. Suppressive famciclovir therapy was compared to suppressive valaciclovir therapy in the Wald 2006 study. Famciclovir 250 mg twice daily was compared to valaciclovir 500 mg once daily for the suppression of clinical genital herpes recurrences and HSV shedding. 18. Compliance rates were high, with 78–96% of participants reporting adherence greater than 85%. 19. Suppressive valaciclovir therapy was compared to suppressive acyclovir therapy in the Johnston 2012 study. Valaciclovir 500 mg once daily was compared to acyclovir 800 mg three times daily. 20. WHO guidelines (Recommendations 5 and 6) for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus highlight the importance of suppressive therapy for reducing recurrence and improving quality of life.
